Optimal Sample Sizes for a Budget Constrained Contrast

Source: R/seq_budget.R
seq_budget_optimal.Rd

For planning before any data are collected: given assumed population standard deviations, returns the sample sizes that estimate a linear contrast of K population means as precisely as a fixed budget allows when an observation costs a different amount in each population. This is Theorem 1 of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025).

Usage

seq_budget_optimal(contrast_weights, sigmas, cost_per_group, budget)

Arguments

contrast_weights

Numeric vector of length K (at least 2) giving the contrast coefficients \(c_i\), one per population, not all zero. The article takes them to sum to zero (a contrast); the allocation holds for any linear combination, so the sum is not checked. A population with a weight of zero is allocated no observations.

sigmas

Numeric vector of length K giving the assumed population standard deviations \(\sigma_i\), each positive, in the order of the weights.

cost_per_group

Numeric vector of length K giving the cost \(a_i\) of one observation from each population, each positive, in the units of budget. The order is that of the weights.

budget

The total budget \(A_0\): a single positive number.

Value

A list with two components: n_per_group, a numeric vector of length K with the optimal sample sizes \(n_{i0}\) (not rounded; their total cost equals budget), and minimum_variance, the minimized variance \(V_o\) of the contrast estimator.

Details

Write the contrast as \(\psi = \sum_{i=1}^{K} c_i \mu_i\), estimated by \(\hat{\psi} = \sum_{i=1}^{K} c_i \bar{X}_i\) with variance \(\sum_{i=1}^{K} c_i^2 \sigma_i^2 / n_i\) (Equations 3 to 5 of the article). With a cost of \(a_i\) per observation from population \(i\) and a budget \(A_0\), the sample sizes that minimize that variance subject to \(\sum_{i=1}^{K} a_i n_i = A_0\) are (Equation 12) $$n_{i0} = \frac{A_0 \, |c_i| \, \sigma_i} {\sqrt{a_i} \, \sum_{l=1}^{K} |c_l| \, \sigma_l \, \sqrt{a_l}}, \quad i = 1, \ldots, K,$$ and the minimized variance is (Equation 13) $$V_o = \frac{1}{A_0} \left( \sum_{i=1}^{K} |c_i| \, \sigma_i \, \sqrt{a_i} \right)^2.$$ A population receives more observations when its scores vary more, when its weight in the contrast is larger, and when it is cheaper to sample. Minimizing the variance is what maximizes the power of the article's noninferiority, superiority, and equivalence tests for a given budget.

The sizes are returned as they come out of the formula, not rounded. Rounding every size up would cost more than the budget: in the article's example (three populations, 30 per observation, a budget of 10,000; p. 430) each \(n_{i0}\) is 111.11, which holds when the products \(|c_i| \sigma_i\) are equal, and 111 per group costs 9,990 where 112 per group would cost 10,080.

In practice the standard deviations are not known. seq_budget replaces them with the sample standard deviations and updates the allocation as observations arrive, and seq_budget_sensitivity shows by simulation how close that procedure comes to the allocation returned here.

The three vector arguments are matched by position. If more than one of them is named, the names must be the same and in the same order; otherwise the function stops, so that a vector named in another order is not applied to the wrong populations.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

Luh, W. M., & Guo, J. H. (2016). Sample size planning for the noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast with cost considerations. Psychological Methods, 21(1), 13–34. doi:10.1037/met0000039

See also

seq_budget for the sequential procedure when the standard deviations are unknown. In DMAR, ss_seq_c reports the same cost optimal allocation for a sequential fixed-width interval.

Other seq_budget: decide_seq_budget, seq_budget(), seq_budget_next(), seq_budget_pilot(), seq_budget_sensitivity()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Two new training formats (groups 1 and 3) against the current one
# (group 2): the weights 1, -2, 1 give twice the difference between the
# average of the new formats and the current format. An observation costs
# 38, 15, and 10 in the three groups, and the budget is 5,000 (the normal
# row of Table 1 in the article).
seq_budget_optimal(
  contrast_weights = c(1, -2, 1),
  sigmas = c(4.5, 0.9, 1),
  cost_per_group = c(38, 15, 10),
  budget = 5000
)
#> $n_per_group
#> [1] 96.37295 61.35660 41.74788
#> 
#> $minimum_variance
#> [1] 0.2868806
#> 

# The article's example on p. 430: equal costs, and equal products of
# weight and standard deviation.
seq_budget_optimal(
  contrast_weights = c(-1, 0.5, 0.5),
  sigmas = c(1, 2, 2),
  cost_per_group = c(30, 30, 30),
  budget = 10000
)$n_per_group
#> [1] 111.1111 111.1111 111.1111
